## Do international institutions matter? {background-image="./Images/background-scales_justice_v3.png" .center}

![](Images/03_1-Boxing_v6.png){style="display: block; margin: 0 auto"}

::: notes

Our interest this week has been to flesh out our theoretical understanding of what impact international institutions can be expected to have on actual state behavior

<br>

Mearsheimer, speaking for the realists, argued that international behavior follows the balance of power

- Powerful states make institutions to enshrine or expand their power

- Weak states follow those rules because they are weak, not because they are law

<br>

Keohane, speaking for the institutionalists, argued that self-interested states can use institutions to facilitate meaningful cooperation

- And by cooperation we mean a very hard test of "policy coordination"

- "intergovernmental cooperation takes place when the policies actually followed by one government are regarded by its partners as facilitating realization of their own objectives, as the results of a process of policy coordination (51-52).

<br>

Our job for today is to use empirical cases to examine the expectations of each theory

- Ultimately, theory is only as useful as it is accurate in making predictions about the real world

- SO, does reality look more like offensive realism or institutionalism? Let's find out!

<br>

**SLIDE**:

<br>

*Other Notes*

- Some of the debate relates to defining the key concept: North's "institution" vs Mearsheimer's "international institution" vs Keohane's "international regime"

- Some of the debate relates to the different outcomes: Mearsheimer's test seems to be focused on stopping wars vs Keohane's "cooperation" vs "discord"

:::
